evidence.note: Opening strategy: build the smallest complete implementation matching the client's calls, then 'expand where the hidden requirements are likely to probe' — an explicit breadth-first-then-deepen plan.
Chose a proper AST evaluator over string-eval because it's the shared enabler for spills/LET/LAMBDA/ranges/errors — investing in a foundation that unlocks broad coverage cheaply.

Single broad build: ~160+ functions across every catalog family plus locale translations, and all endpoints (collab, pivots, goal seek, validation, conditional formatting, names, CSV/XLSX). Locks in wide end-to-end coverage before perfecting any corner.
Post-run triage patches 'concentrated and mechanical' failures rather than over-investing in one area — proportionate effort.
Explicit depth pass on 'areas the hidden suite is likely to vary' (deep chains, multi-array MAP, BYCOL, OFFSET) — a breadth-vs-depth call tied to expected graded weight.

Deepened high-value/high-risk areas: perf chain, persistence-across-restart, and XLSX cached-value openpyxl round-trip (a graded corpus). Depth directed to likely-graded surfaces, though the XLSX fix was pursued to completion without an explicit payoff time-box.

reasoning: The agent secured broad end-to-end coverage of the huge function catalog and endpoint surface first (steps 25-28), then made explicit, payoff-aware depth choices — hardening high-variance formula areas and high-value graded surfaces like XLSX round-trip and persistence (steps 56, 64-87). This is precisely the level-8 pattern: explicit breadth-vs-depth calls tied to likely graded weight, breadth locked in early, then deepening high-value/high-risk areas. It falls short of 10 because there is little evidence of iteratively revisiting the allocation or consciously cutting/deferring low-yield perfectionism (e.g., the XLSX fix was carried to completion without a stated marginal-value tradeoff).
